paragraphs.heading: The most common value
paragraphs.text: The mode is the value that turns up most often in a set of data. Like the mean and the median, it is a summary statistic for central tendency, the center of a group of values. In a sample made of 1, 3, 6 four times, 7 twice, 12 twice and 17, the number 6 occurs more often than any other, so 6 is the mode.

paragraphs.heading: More than one mode
paragraphs.text: A data set can have more than one mode. In the list 1, 1, 2, 4, 4, the values 1 and 4 tie for most common, so the mode is not unique and the list is called bimodal. A set with more than two modes is called multimodal. The extreme case is a uniform distribution, where every value is equally common.

paragraphs.heading: It works for names
paragraphs.text: The mode has an advantage the mean and median lack: it works for nominal data, labels that are neither numbers nor ranked. In a sample of Korean family names, Kim might occur more often than any other name, which would make Kim the mode. Plurality voting follows the same logic: a single most common choice decides the winner, while a tie between several modes needs some tie-breaking rule.

paragraphs.heading: Peaks in a distribution
paragraphs.text: For a discrete random variable, the mode is the value where the probability mass function is highest, the value most likely to come up in a sample. For a continuous distribution, a mode is usually taken to be any point where the probability density function reaches a local peak. A distribution with several peaks has several modes and is called multimodal, while one with a single peak is unimodal.

paragraphs.heading: Finding it in measurements
paragraphs.text: Raw measurements from a continuous distribution, such as 0.935 and 1.211, never match exactly, so each value appears once and the plain mode tells you nothing. The usual fix is to sort the data into intervals of equal width, as when drawing a histogram. The mode is then the point where the histogram peaks. Another approach, kernel density estimation, blurs the data points into a smooth curve whose peak gives an estimate of the mode.

paragraphs.heading: Next to the mean and median
paragraphs.text: In symmetric distributions with one peak, such as the normal distribution, the mode, mean and median coincide. In highly skewed distributions, though, the mode can be very different from the other two. Except in very small samples, the mode is not thrown off by outliers such as rare false readings; the median is robust too, while the mean is rather sensitive. When a continuous distribution has a single peak, the median often falls between the other two, roughly one third of the way from the mean toward the mode.
